claims.claim: Maternal and child health is the public health field focused on the health of mothers, infants, and children; in the United States, HRSA's Maternal and Child Health Bureau frames the field with the mission to improve the health and well-being of America's mothers, children, and families.

WHO defines maternal health as the health of women during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postnatal period, and states that most maternal deaths are preventable with timely management by a skilled health professional working in a supportive environment.

The Maternal and Child Health Bureau takes a life course approach to improving the health and well-being of mothers, children, and families, the field's core argument that early life shapes later health.

WHO states that care by skilled health professionals before, during, and after childbirth can save the lives of women and newborns; the MCH care continuum runs from preconception through prenatal care, birth, postpartum, and early childhood.

Prenatal care is the health care a woman receives during pregnancy, including checkups and testing, lets providers spot health problems early, and is typically provided by an obstetrician or a midwife.

Routine childhood immunization reaches most of the world's children: WHO reports DTP3 (diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis, third dose) coverage of 85 percent in 2025, while 13.5 million children received no vaccines at all that year.

WIC, the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children, provides healthy foods, nutrition education, breastfeeding support, and referrals for low-income pregnant, postpartum, and breastfeeding women and children up to age five.

Globally, the under-five mortality rate fell to 37.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024, less than half its 2000 level, with an estimated 4.9 million children under five dying in 2024; progress has slowed since 2015, and more than 80 percent of under-five deaths occur in sub-Saharan Africa and Southern Asia.

The maternal mortality ratio dropped by about 40 percent worldwide between 2000 and 2023, yet about 260,000 women died during and following pregnancy and childbirth in 2023, with over 90 percent of maternal deaths occurring in low- and lower-middle-income countries.

The MCH workforce spans obstetricians and midwives (prenatal care and delivery), pediatricians (committed to the health of infants, children, adolescents, and young adults), nurses, and community health workers who serve as trusted links between communities and services.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Maternal death estimates differ by vintage: the WHO Maternal health topic page still cites about 287,000 deaths in 2020, while the April 2025 maternal mortality fact sheet reports about 260,000 deaths in 2023.
positions: About 287,000 maternal deaths in 2020 (WHO maternal health topic page)
About 260,000 maternal deaths in 2023 (WHO maternal mortality fact sheet, 7 April 2025)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson cites only the most recent WHO fact sheet figure (260,000 in 2023) with its date, and does not repeat the older 2020 figure.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Progress phrasing differs across WHO pages: the child health topic page says the number of children dying before age 5 was halved from 2000 to 2017, while the May 2026 fact sheet says the 2024 under-five mortality rate (37.4 per 1,000) is less than half its 2000 level.
positions: Halved from 2000 to 2017 (WHO child health topic page)
2024 rate less than half the 2000 level (WHO child mortality fact sheet, 1 May 2026)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both statements point the same direction; the lesson uses the newer fact-sheet figure with its date.

sourceRecords.title: About Us: Mission, Vision, and Work
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Health Resources and Services Administration, Maternal and Child Health Bureau (MCHB)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via a Wayback Machine capture (web.archive.org/web/2025/) because hrsa.gov returned 403 to direct fetch; canonical URL recorded. Supports: the MCHB mission to improve the health and well-being of America's mothers, children, and families; the bureau's life course approach to the health of mothers, children, and families; and the field's U.S. federal framing. Short mission phrase quoted with attribution; prose otherwise original.

sourceRecords.title: Maternal health (Health topics)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22. Supports the WHO definition that maternal health refers to the health of women during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postnatal period; that most maternal deaths are preventable with timely management by a skilled health professional working in a supportive environment; and the dated 2020 death figure (287,000), which the lesson supersedes with the 2023 fact-sheet figure.

sourceRecords.title: Maternal mortality (Fact sheet)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22; fact sheet dated 7 April 2025. Supports: about 260,000 women died during and following pregnancy and childbirth in 2023; the maternal mortality ratio dropped about 40 percent worldwide between 2000 and 2023; over 90 percent of maternal deaths occurred in low- and lower-middle-income countries; and care by skilled health professionals before, during, and after childbirth can save the lives of women and newborns.

sourceRecords.title: Child mortality (under 5 years) (Fact sheet)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22; fact sheet dated 1 May 2026. Supports: an estimated 4.9 million children under five died in 2024; the global under-five mortality rate of 37.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024, less than half its 2000 level; about 60 percent decline since 1990; slowed progress since 2015 with stagnation between 2022 and 2024; neonatal deaths (first 28 days) as 47 percent of under-five deaths; and more than 80 percent of under-five deaths in sub-Saharan Africa and Southern Asia.

sourceRecords.title: Child health (Health topics)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22. Supports: protecting and improving the health of children is of fundamental importance; dramatic progress in improving child health over recent decades; that child health, growth, and development are inseparable; and that a great deal of work remains.

sourceRecords.title: Immunization coverage (Fact sheet)
sourceRecords.notes: Source id reused from the phase-4 source-registry.json with an identical URL. Read directly 2026-08-22; fact sheet dated 15 July 2026. Supports: DTP3 (third dose of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis vaccine) coverage of 85 percent in 2025; first-dose measles vaccine coverage of 84 percent in 2025; and 13.5 million zero-dose children (no vaccinations at all) in 2025. Used for the immunization-program line in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: Prenatal Care
sourceRecords.provider: MedlinePlus, U.S. National Library of Medicine (NIH)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22. Supports: prenatal care is the health care a woman gets while pregnant, including checkups and prenatal testing; it helps keep mother and fetus healthy and lets providers spot problems early; and it is typically provided by a provider specializing in pregnancy and delivery, such as an obstetrician or a midwife.

sourceRecords.title: WIC: USDA's Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food and Nutrition Service
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22. Supports: WIC is the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children; it provides healthy foods, personalized nutrition education, breastfeeding support, and referrals to other services; and it serves women who are pregnant, recently pregnant, or breastfeeding, plus infants and children up to age five.

sourceRecords.title: Community Health Workers (Section of the APHA)
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22. Supports the APHA-adopted definition that a community health worker is a frontline public health worker who is a trusted member of, or has an unusually close understanding of, the community served, and who serves as a liaison or link between health and social services and the community. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: About the American Academy of Pediatrics
sourceRecords.notes: Read directly 2026-08-22. Supports the pediatrician line: the AAP describes its 67,000 pediatricians as committed to the optimal physical, mental, and social health and well-being for all infants, children, adolescents, and young adults. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.
